rows.requirement: Distinguish RNA A/U/G/C from coding DNA A/T/G/C without equating unprocessed genomic and mature transcript sequences.

evidence.excerpt: In the standard code, four RNA letters, A, U, G and C, give 4 × 4 × 4 = 64 possible codons. Of these, 61 specify the 20 common amino acids and UAA, UAG and UGA signal termination. Several codons can specify the same amino acid; methionine has AUG and tryptophan has UGG. A third-position change often preserves the amino acid, but this is not true for every codon.

Coding-DNA reports use T where the corresponding RNA sequence uses U. Matching them requires the coding strand and a specified processed transcript; an unprocessed genomic stretch can contain introns. In variant notation, c. numbers coding-DNA positions and p. describes a protein consequence relative to a named reference. The symbols fs, Ter and * denote frameshift and termination. HGVS places predicted protein consequences in parentheses when RNA or protein has not been analysed.

evidence.excerpt: For ordinary cap-dependent eukaryotic initiation, the translation machinery scans from the front of the message and the sequence around AUG helps determine initiation. It need not use the first AUG. Initiation commonly supplies methionine; subsequent processing can change the protein end. Bacterial initiation and mitochondrial translation have their own context, and NCBI lists alternative initiation codons. An AUG within an already translated frame normally adds methionine rather than starting a second protein.

sourceScope: OpenStax 15.5 initiation/termination passages and NCBI alternative-initiation annotations; no universal first-AUG rule.

rows.requirement: Describe what the Crick 1961 bacteriophage experiments established about triplets and compensating frame changes, without turning three-base deletion into a guarantee of normal function.

evidence.excerpt: Two historical experiments addressed different questions. Crick and colleagues studied bacteriophage genetics in 1961; combinations of three changes could partly restore function when the individual changes did not. The authors argued for a coding ratio of three or a multiple of three, with three more likely, rather than guaranteeing that every three-base deletion is harmless. Nirenberg's 1968 Nobel lecture recounts his work with Matthaei in which synthetic poly-U directed polyphenylalanine synthesis in cell-free E. coli extracts. That connected U-rich RNA with phenylalanine, while UUU is the corresponding codon in the standard table.

sourceScope: Crick 1961 NLM scan, targeted introduction and coding-ratio/triple-mutant sections; printed p.1230 viewed. Nirenberg 1968 lecture targeted text and printed p.374 viewed. No whole original paper read; Nirenberg 1961 original remains unread.

rows.requirement: Explain that the code is nearly universal while retaining code-table exceptions.

evidence.excerpt: The standard table is nearly universal, not universal. Human mitochondria encode 13 proteins and use a different translation table. NCBI table 2 assigns UGA to tryptophan and AUA to methionine, with AGA and AGG as termination signals. A nuclear variant should not be interpreted with that mitochondrial table. A table assignment also differs from demonstrating the release mechanism: Krüger 2023 tested release at AGA and AGG in a reconstituted mitochondrial system, and Wakigawa 2026 studied release-factor specificity in cellular translation experiments.

In the exercise, 2 is not divisible by 3, so deleting those bases changes the downstream frame. The fictional standard-code substitution UGG to UGA creates a stop instead of tryptophan. A premature stop can shorten a protein or lead to nonsense-mediated RNA decay; that outcome is not established for every transcript by the variant class alone. GAA and GAG both encode glutamate, illustrating a synonymous substitution. Synonymous does not mean biologically silent: RNA processing can still change. A missense substitution changes an amino acid, while a frameshift changes the later codon grouping and may encounter a premature stop.

evidence.excerpt: MedlinePlus describes many inherited BRCA1 and BRCA2 risk variants as producing a shortened or absent functional product. Frameshift and nonsense examples illustrate ways to disrupt coding information; these examples and their ClinVar entries do not estimate what fraction of all inherited BRCA variants belong to either class. Secondary tumour changes can sometimes restore a BRCA reading frame or repair function. Restoring a frame, demonstrating repair and predicting a clinical drug response remain separate questions.

Sakai 2008 described secondary BRCA2 changes that restored the reading frame in breast and pancreatic cancer models. The selected clones resisted cisplatin and the experimental PARP inhibitor AG14361. A recurrent BRCA2-mutated ovarian tumour with acquired cisplatin resistance also carried a reversion. These examples establish a possible resistance mechanism, rather than a universal frequency across cancers, assays or medicines.

Sakai 2009 studied ovarian cancer cell lines from one BRCA2-variant carrier. A secondary change cancelled an inherited nonsense variant, BRCA2 protein was detectable in resistant lines, and further experiments selected BRCA2-restored clones. Reducing BRCA2 with siRNA made the restored clones and PEO4 cells more sensitive to cisplatin and AG14361. This is evidence from a named cellular model and depletion experiment, rather than a clinical trial selecting a subsequent treatment.

rows.requirement: Explain frameshift-derived new peptides and their relevance in mismatch-repair-deficient cancers without claiming every frameshift makes an exclusive, presented or immunogenic peptide.

evidence.excerpt: Le and colleagues studied pembrolizumab in 86 people with advanced mismatch-repair-deficient cancers across 12 tumour types in 2017. They reported objective radiographic responses in 46 of 86, or 53%; this is a cohort outcome, not the response chance for any particular frameshift. Detailed mutant-peptide T-cell experiments used one responding person, and the peptides that scored positive came from frameshifts. A genomic frameshift alone does not establish natural peptide presentation, T-cell recognition or clinical benefit.
